We do not have a liberal media problem. We do not have a conservative media problem. We have a profit-driven media problem. And no amount of media literacy, no number of fact-checkers, no algorithm adjustment will fix it — because the incentive structure itself is rotten.

Private media companies in the United States generate revenue through attention. Attention is captured through emotion. And the most powerful emotions — fear, outrage, tribal loyalty — are the enemies of nuanced, honest reporting.

This is not a conspiracy. It is simply capitalism functioning as designed in a domain where it should never have been given unchecked dominion.

Consider the facts:

  • Trust in media has collapsed. Gallup reports that Americans' trust in mass media to report the news "fully, accurately, and fairly" has plummeted to historic lows. This is not a failure of the audience. This is a failure of the institution.

  • Consolidation has gutted local news. Over 2,500 newspapers have closed since 2005. Entire communities — we call them "news deserts" — have no local coverage whatsoever. Corporate owners have stripped these outlets for parts, leaving citizens unable to hold their own city councils accountable.

  • Foreign adversaries exploit the vacuum. Russia, China, Iran — they don't need to create disinformation from scratch. They simply amplify the confusion that our own fragmented, sensationalized media environment has already created. A nation that cannot agree on basic facts is a nation vulnerable to manipulation from every direction.

  • The algorithmic ecosystem rewards extremism. The more partisan, the more misleading, the more emotionally charged a piece of content is, the further it travels. Quality journalism — careful, sourced, measured — is structurally disadvantaged in the modern information marketplace.

We are not going to fact-check our way out of this. We are not going to hope the market self-corrects. The market created this problem. The market will not solve it.

The Democratic Case for Public Media Dominance

Now, I know what some of you are thinking. "Government-run media? That sounds like propaganda. That sounds like state television in authoritarian countries."

I hear you. And I want to address that concern directly, because it deserves a serious answer — not a dismissal.

First: we already accept public funding for institutions we consider too important to leave entirely to the market. We publicly fund the military. We publicly fund roads, schools, courts, scientific research, public health. We do this not because government does everything well, but because some functions are so essential to the republic that we cannot allow them to exist only when and where they are profitable.

Is there any function more essential to democracy than an informed citizenry? Madison told us: "A popular government without popular information, or the means of acquiring it, is but a prologue to a farce or a tragedy, or perhaps both." We are living in that prologue right now.

Second: the model works. Look at the BBC — the most trusted news organization in the world, publicly funded for a century, with editorial standards that put every American cable network to shame. Look at Germany's Deutsche Welle. Look at Canada's CBC. Look at Australia's ABC. These are not propaganda outlets. These are pillars of democratic life in their nations. They are proof — living, breathing, daily proof — that public funding and editorial rigor are not contradictions. They are complements.

What do all of these nations understand that we refuse to accept? They understand that information is public infrastructure. Just like clean water, just like highways, just like the court system — the flow of reliable information to citizens is a public good that requires public investment.

Third — and here is the argument I want you to sit with — private media is not "free" from control. It is controlled by money. Every editorial decision at a private outlet is made within the constraints of what owners will permit, what advertisers will tolerate, and what audiences, trained on years of sensationalism, will click.

When a pharmaceutical company spends billions on cable news advertising, do you truly believe coverage of drug pricing is unaffected? When a media conglomerate has business interests before regulatory agencies, do you truly believe their political coverage carries no bias? When a billionaire purchases a newspaper, do you truly believe their worldview doesn't seep into editorial decisions?

The question has never been "controlled or not controlled." The question is: controlled by whom, and accountable to whom?

A corporation is accountable to its shareholders. A government institution, in a democracy, is accountable to you.

The Vision: An American News Service

So let me describe what I am proposing — not in vague terms, but concretely.

The American News Service would be a federally chartered, publicly funded institution with a singular mandate: to provide the American people with comprehensive, accurate, and accessible journalism at every level — local, state, national, and international.

Its scale would be unprecedented. Not a shoestring operation like our current CPB, starved of funding and perpetually terrified of Congressional reprisal. This would be an institution funded at a level commensurate with the importance of its mission — comparable to what the BBC represents in British public life or what the Associated Press once represented as the default source of straight reporting.

We are the wealthiest nation in the history of the world. We spend $850 billion annually on defense. We can afford to invest seriously — ambitiously — in the information infrastructure that democracy requires to function.

Here are the pillars:

1. Universal Local Coverage

Every county in America would have access to dedicated reporters covering local government, local courts, local schools, and local business. No more news deserts. No more city councils operating in darkness. No more school boards making decisions that affect your children with no journalist in the room.

The collapse of local news is not just an inconvenience. Research from Notre Dame, from Duke, from the Brookings Institution has demonstrated that when local news disappears, municipal borrowing costs rise, corruption increases, voter participation drops, and civic engagement withers. Local journalism is the capillary system of democracy. We have allowed it to hemorrhage, and the body politic is weakening because of it.

The American News Service would rebuild that system from the ground up.

2. Nonpartisan, Standards-Based Reporting

The institution would operate under a strict editorial charter — publicly available, legally binding — modeled on the best practices of the BBC, the AP, and Reuters. Sourcing standards. Correction policies. Separation of news and commentary. Transparency about methodology.

Not opinion. Not entertainment. Not infotainment. News. Reported by professional journalists held to professional standards, with public accountability mechanisms that no private outlet would ever voluntarily adopt.

3. A Counterweight to Disinformation

In an era of deepfakes, AI-generated content, and foreign information warfare, Americans need a trusted default — a place they can go and know that what they are reading has been verified, sourced, and held to a standard. The American News Service would serve as that anchor.

Not the only source. But the reliable source. The baseline. The institution that, when the crisis comes — and the crises will come — the nation can turn to and trust.

4. Structural Independence Through Governance Design

Now — and this is critical — the governance would be designed to insulate editorial operations from political interference. An independent board of directors, appointed through staggered terms across administrations, confirmed by supermajority Senate vote. An inspector general for editorial integrity. Legally codified protections for journalists within the institution, modeled on judicial independence principles.

Would this be perfect? No. No institution is. But consider what we have now: media outlets with zero structural accountability to the public interest. Zero editorial standards that carry legal weight. Zero obligation to accuracy, fairness, or completeness.

We are not comparing a government institution to some platonic ideal of a free press. We are comparing it to what actually exists — a landscape of partisan infotainment, clickbait factories, and corporate mouthpieces masquerading as journalism.

Confronting the Objections

Let me turn now to the objections, because I respect this audience enough to engage with them honestly.

"This violates the First Amendment."

No. It does not. The First Amendment prohibits the government from restricting speech. It does not prohibit the government from speaking. The government already publishes vast amounts of information. It funds research. It funds the Voice of America for international audiences. Creating a public news institution does not prevent a single private outlet from publishing a single word.

The First Amendment protects the right of every American to speak and publish freely. It does not guarantee that Rupert Murdoch's business model is the best way to inform a democracy.

"Government media will become propaganda."

This is the most serious objection, and it deserves the most serious answer.

Yes, the risk exists. And that is precisely why governance design matters so much. The BBC has operated for over a century with public funding and maintained editorial independence through the Falklands War, through Iraq, through Brexit — often to the fury of the very government that funds it. Structure matters. Legal protections matter. Cultural norms of editorial independence matter.

But let me ask you this: what do you call what we have now? When a cable network functions as the de facto communications arm of a political party — when its hosts coordinate messaging with political operatives — when it amplifies claims it knows to be false because those claims serve its audience's partisan appetites — what is that, if not propaganda?

The difference is that government propaganda, in a democracy, can be subjected to oversight, FOIA requests, inspector general investigations, and Congressional accountability. Corporate propaganda operates in the dark, answerable to no one but the bottom line.

I am not arguing that government control carries no risk. I am arguing that the risks of our current system are not hypothetical — they are here, now, measurable, and devastating — and we have decided, out of a reflexive libertarian instinct, to simply accept those risks as the cost of freedom.

That is not wisdom. That is complacency dressed up as principle.

"Competition and the free market of ideas will produce the best outcomes."

This is the argument I find most frustrating, because it sounds so elegant in theory and has failed so catastrophically in practice.

The "free market of ideas" assumes that consumers can readily distinguish quality information from junk. It assumes that accurate reporting is rewarded by the market and inaccurate reporting is punished. It assumes that the barriers to entry are low enough that good journalism can always find an audience and a revenue stream.

None of these assumptions hold in the modern information environment. Not one.

Disinformation is cheaper to produce than quality journalism. It travels faster on social media. It generates more engagement. And consumers, who are not specialists in every subject, often cannot distinguish between a well-sourced investigation and a convincing fabrication — especially when the fabrication confirms what they already believe.

The free market of ideas has given us anti-vaccine movements, election denialism, and climate change doubt persisting decades after scientific consensus. The market has spoken, and it has said: "Outrage is more profitable than accuracy."

We do not let the "free market" determine the safety of our medications, the structural integrity of our bridges, or the training of our airline pilots. We impose standards, because some things are too important to leave to the profit motive alone. Why do we treat the information that citizens use to govern themselves as less important than the safety of a bridge?

The Moral Urgency

My friends, I want to end on this:

Self-governance — real, meaningful self-governance — requires a shared foundation of fact. Not shared opinions. Not shared ideology. Shared facts. A shared understanding of what is happening, to whom, and why.

That foundation is crumbling. You can feel it. Every Thanksgiving dinner that devolves into a screaming match. Every friendship strained by political disagreements that aren't really about politics but about people living in completely different factual universes. Every election cycle that feels less like a democratic choice and more like a tribal war conducted in mutual incomprehension.

This is what the collapse of trusted information infrastructure looks like. Not tanks in the streets. Not a dramatic coup. Just a slow, agonizing erosion of the shared reality that makes democracy possible.

And into that vacuum rush the demagogues, the conspiracy entrepreneurs, the foreign adversaries, and the corporations that have learned to monetize confusion itself.

We built public schools because we understood that an educated citizenry was too important to leave to the market. We built public libraries because we understood that access to knowledge must be universal. We built public roads, public courts, public health systems — all because we recognized that some goods are so fundamental to the functioning of a free society that they must be guaranteed, not merely hoped for.

It is time — past time — to extend that same principle to the information that citizens need to govern themselves.

The American News Service would not silence any voice. It would not close any outlet. It would not restrict any freedom. It would simply ensure that amidst the noise, the spin, and the fury — there exists one institution, funded by the people, accountable to the people, dedicated to telling the people the truth.

Not a party's truth. Not a corporation's truth. Not an algorithm's truth. The truth — as best as honest, professional, accountable journalists can determine it.

Is that not worth fighting for? Is that not worth building? Is that not what a nation that still calls itself a democracy owes to its citizens?

I believe it is. And I believe that if we have the courage to build it, future generations will look back and wonder what took us so long.

Thank you.
